# Section 2: Statement of Need — Draft

---

## Three Opening-Paragraph Options (pick one)

**Option A — Lead with a single striking statistic**

> In [ZIP/neighborhood], [X]% of [population] [experience/lack access to] [condition] — [X] times the [state/national] average ([source, year]). Despite [existing effort], [gap]: [number] residents remain [unserved/on waitlists/without access], and the problem is [growing/unchanged] since [year]. [Organization] proposes to address this gap by [core intervention] for [number] [population] over [grant period].

**Option B — Lead with community voice**

> When [Organization] surveyed [number] [population] in [year], the most common response was [quote or paraphrase]: "[Direct quote from resident/stakeholder]." The data confirm what residents already know: [key statistic, source, year]. Yet [gap statement]. This project will [core intervention] for [number] [population] who currently [barrier].

**Option C — Lead with trend/urgency**

> Between [year] and [year], [indicator] in [place] [rose/fell] by [X]% ([source]), outpacing [comparison geography] by [factor]. Left unaddressed, [projected consequence]. [Organization] will [core intervention], reaching [number] [population] annually in the [ZIP codes/neighborhoods] most affected.

---

## Full Draft (~600 words)

[Chosen opening paragraph from above.]

**The scope of the problem.** [Community/region] is home to [population number] residents across [geography: ZIP codes, census tracts, county] ([ACS/Census, year]). Of these, [X]% live below [income threshold] ([source, year]), and [X]% identify as [demographic breakdown relevant to disparities] ([source, year]). [Population subgroup] faces compounding barriers: [barrier 1], [barrier 2], and [barrier 3], each of which increases risk for [core problem the grant addresses].

[Core problem] is well documented in the area. [Indicator 1] stands at [X]%, compared with [Y]% statewide and [Z]% nationally ([source, year]). [Indicator 2] has [worsened/remained stagnant] over the past [number] years, [rising/falling] from [baseline] in [year] to [current figure] in [year] ([source]). The [agency/system] reports that [related system-level data point — e.g., ER visits, school suspensions, eviction filings] reached [number] in [most recent year available] ([source, year]), a [X]% increase over [comparison year].

**Disparities within the community.** The burden is not evenly distributed. [Subpopulation A] experiences [indicator] at [X] times the rate of [subpopulation B] ([source, year]). [Geographic pocket — e.g., census tract, neighborhood] shows the highest concentration: [data point] ([source, year]). [One additional disparity data point with source.]

**Service gaps.** Although [existing programs/providers] offer [service type], capacity falls short of demand. [Provider/agency] currently maintains a waitlist of [number] individuals, with an average wait time of [duration] ([source or internal data, year]). [Number] of the [total] eligible residents received [service] in the most recent reporting period ([source, year]) — a coverage rate of just [X]%. No provider in [area] currently offers [specific service or modality your program will deliver], leaving [population] without [critical resource].

**Community input.** These findings align with direct input from the people most affected. In [month/year], [Organization] conducted [method — survey, focus groups, listening sessions, town hall] with [number] [population]. [X]% of respondents identified [problem/need] as their top concern, and [X]% reported [specific barrier — e.g., transportation, cost, language, stigma] as the primary reason they had not accessed services. [Optional: one brief direct quote.] Letters of support from [partner organizations, elected officials, community leaders] (see Appendix [X]) further confirm the urgency and the community's readiness for this intervention.

**Why now.** [Triggering event, policy change, funding cliff, or new data release] has created both heightened need and a window of opportunity. [One sentence explaining the trigger, with source if applicable.] Without targeted intervention, [projected consequence — e.g., "an estimated [number] additional [population] will [negative outcome] by [year] ([source])"].

---

## Data-Pull Checklist

Gather the following before finalizing. Each row gives you the source and suggested phrasing to drop straight into the draft.

**Demographics & Poverty**
- [ ] Total population in service area → U.S. Census / ACS 5-year, most recent → *"[Place] is home to [X] residents (ACS [year])."*
- [ ] Poverty rate → ACS Table S1701 → *"[X]% live below the federal poverty level, compared with [Y]% statewide."*
- [ ] Racial/ethnic breakdown (if relevant to disparities) → ACS Table B03002 → *"[X]% identify as [group]."*

**Core Problem Indicators**
- [ ] Primary indicator, local → [your state/county data portal, school district, health department] → *"[Indicator] stands at [X]%, compared with [Y]% statewide ([source, year])."*
- [ ] Primary indicator, trend → same source, two time points → *"[Indicator] [rose/fell] from [X] in [year] to [Y] in [year]."*
- [ ] Secondary indicator → [relevant system — ER, courts, schools, shelters] → *"[System] reported [number] [events] in [year], a [X]% increase since [year]."*

**Disparities**
- [ ] Subpopulation disparity rate → [state/county disaggregated data] → *"[Subgroup] experiences [indicator] at [X] times the rate of [comparison group]."*
- [ ] Geographic hotspot → census tract or ZIP-level data → *"In [tract/ZIP], [indicator] reaches [X]%."*

**Service Gaps**
- [ ] Waitlist or unmet demand → partner agency or internal records → *"[Provider] maintains a waitlist of [number], averaging [duration]."*
- [ ] Coverage rate → program data or needs assessment → *"Only [X]% of eligible residents received [service] in [year]."*
- [ ] Missing service type → landscape scan or 211 data → *"No provider in [area] currently offers [service]."*

**Community Voice**
- [ ] Survey/focus group topline → internal data → *"[X]% of respondents identified [need] as their top concern (n=[X], [year])."*
- [ ] Barrier cited → same source → *"[X]% reported [barrier] as the primary obstacle to accessing services."*
- [ ] Direct quote → survey or focus group transcript → *"As one resident stated, '[quote].'"*
- [ ] Letters of support → partners, officials → referenced in text, included in appendix

**Urgency / "Why Now"**
- [ ] Triggering event or trend → news, policy brief, data release → *"Since [event/date], [consequence], creating an urgent need for [intervention]."*
- [ ] Projected consequence if unaddressed → credible projection or extrapolation → *"Without action, an estimated [number] [population] will [outcome] by [year]."*

# Section 2: Statement of Need — Polished Draft

## Paste-Ready Version (No Subheadings)

In Riverton's 12345 ZIP code, 28% of children ages 0–8 read below a sixth-grade functional literacy level — more than double the statewide rate of 12% ([SOURCE, YEAR]). Despite existing services, 150 families remain on waitlists for literacy support, and the problem has worsened steadily since [INDICATOR1_BASEYEAR]. [ORG_NAME] proposes to close this gap through a culturally responsive family literacy program serving 400 children ages 0–8 and their caregivers over 24 months.

Riverton is home to 42,000 residents ([ACS_YEAR] American Community Survey). Nearly one in four — 22.5% — live below the federal poverty level, compared with [POVERTY_STATE]% statewide, and [DEMO_PCT]% identify as [DEMO_GROUP]. These families face compounding barriers — [BARRIER1], [BARRIER2], and [BARRIER3] — each of which is a well-documented predictor of low early literacy. Research consistently shows that children who are not reading at grade level by third grade are four times more likely to drop out of high school (Annie E. Casey Foundation, 2010), making early intervention essential.

The local data are unambiguous. Low literacy among Riverton's youngest residents stands at 28%, against 12% statewide and [INDICATOR1_NATL]% nationally ([INDICATOR1_SOURCE]). That rate has climbed from [INDICATOR1_BASE]% in [INDICATOR1_BASEYEAR], with no sign of reversal. At the systems level, [INDICATOR2_NAME] reached [INDICATOR2_NUM] in [INDICATOR2_YEAR] ([INDICATOR2_SOURCE]), a [INDICATOR2_CHANGE]% increase over [INDICATOR2_COMPYEAR] — a pattern that mirrors and reinforces the literacy crisis.

The burden falls unevenly. [DISPARITY_GROUP] children experience low literacy at [DISPARITY_FACTOR] times the rate of [DISPARITY_COMPARE] ([DISPARITY_SOURCE]). Within Riverton, [HOTSPOT_GEO] shows the highest concentration, where low literacy reaches [HOTSPOT_RATE]%.

Although area providers offer some programming, capacity falls far short of demand. [WAITLIST_PROVIDER] currently carries a waitlist of 150 families, with an average wait of [WAITLIST_DURATION]. In the most recent reporting period, only [COVERAGE_NUM] of [COVERAGE_TOTAL] eligible children received structured literacy services — a coverage rate of just [COVERAGE_PCT]% ([COVERAGE_SOURCE]). Critically, no provider in Riverton offers a family literacy model that engages both children and caregivers simultaneously, leaving families without the dual-generation approach most supported by evidence.

Residents confirm what the numbers show. In [SURVEY_YEAR], [ORG_NAME] conducted a [SURVEY_METHOD] with 89 caregivers in the 12345 ZIP code. [SURVEY_TOPCONCERN_PCT]% identified early literacy as their top concern, and [SURVEY_BARRIER_PCT]% cited [SURVEY_BARRIER] as the primary reason they had not accessed help. As one parent stated, "My child falls behind every year because we can't get help close by." Letters of support from partner organizations and community leaders (Appendix [APPENDIX_REF]) reinforce both the urgency and the community's readiness for a new approach.

[TRIGGER_EVENT] has sharpened the need and opened a window for action. Without targeted intervention, an estimated [PROJECTION_NUM] additional children in Riverton will enter kindergarten without foundational literacy skills by [PROJECTION_YEAR] ([PROJECTION_SOURCE]). This project addresses the right problem, in the right community, at the right time.

Riverton Literacy Project will implement a culturally responsive family literacy program that serves 400 children ages 0–8 and their caregivers over 24 months in the 12345 ZIP code. The program is built on a dual-generation model: rather than targeting children or adults in isolation, every activity engages the caregiver-child pair together, strengthening the home literacy environment that research identifies as the single strongest predictor of early reading success (National Early Literacy Panel, 2008). The design draws on [EVIDENCE_BASE_NAME], an evidence-based framework shown to [EVIDENCE_BASE_OUTCOME] in [EVIDENCE_BASE_POPULATION] ([EVIDENCE_BASE_SOURCE]).

The program operates in three phases. In Phase 1 — Intake and Assessment (months 1–3) — staff will recruit families through [REFERRAL_PARTNERS] and conduct individualized literacy assessments using [ASSESSMENT_TOOL] for children and [CAREGIVER_ASSESSMENT_TOOL] for caregivers. Each family will receive a Family Literacy Plan that sets personalized benchmarks and identifies the services best matched to their needs. Riverton Literacy Project expects to enroll [COHORT_SIZE] families per cohort, with [COHORT_NUM] cohorts launched across the grant period.

Phase 2 — Core Programming (months 2–20) — is the heart of the model and contains three interlocking activity tracks.

Track A: Interactive Literacy Sessions. Each caregiver-child pair will attend [SESSION_FREQ] structured sessions of [SESSION_LENGTH] minutes over [SESSION_WEEKS] weeks, held at [SITE_LOCATIONS]. Sessions follow a consistent arc: shared reading using culturally relevant texts, guided vocabulary and comprehension activities, and a take-home practice component. Groups are capped at [GROUP_SIZE] families to allow individualized coaching. Over 24 months, Riverton Literacy Project will deliver approximately [TOTAL_SESSIONS] sessions.

Track B: Caregiver Skill-Building Workshops. Concurrently, caregivers participate in [WORKSHOP_NUM] workshops focused on supporting literacy at home. Topics include dialogic reading techniques, navigating the school system, and accessing community resources. Workshops are offered in [LANGUAGES] and scheduled during [SCHEDULE_DETAIL] to reduce barriers identified in our community survey — primarily [BARRIER1] and [BARRIER2]. [CHILDCARE_PLAN] is provided during all workshop hours.

Track C: Home-Based Literacy Coaching. Each enrolled family receives [HOMEVISIT_NUM] home visits over the program cycle from a trained literacy coach. Coaches model reading strategies in the family's own environment, distribute age-appropriate book bundles ([BOOKS_PER_FAMILY] books per family), and troubleshoot barriers to daily reading practice. Home visits are especially critical for the [HOMEVISIT_RATIONALE] families who face [BARRIER3] and are least likely to attend site-based programming consistently.

Phase 3 — Transition and Follow-Up (months 18–24) — ensures gains are sustained. Staff conduct exit assessments using the same tools administered at intake, connect families to ongoing community resources such as [TRANSITION_RESOURCES], and administer a [FOLLOWUP_TIMELINE] follow-up check-in after program completion to track retention of skills. Families who do not meet their benchmarks are offered an additional [EXTENDED_SUPPORT] of support before exiting.

The logic model (Appendix [LOGIC_MODEL_APPENDIX]) illustrates how each activity connects to the needs documented in Section 2 and the outcomes defined in Section 6. In summary, the causal pathway is as follows: increased access to structured literacy activities and caregiver coaching leads to more frequent and higher-quality literacy interactions at home, which in turn produces measurable gains in children's foundational reading skills and caregiver confidence.

Riverton Literacy Project will deliver this program with a staffing structure designed for both quality and reach. The team includes a Program Director ([PD_FTE] FTE, [PD_QUALIFICATION]), who provides overall management and funder reporting; [NUM_LITERACY_COACHES] Literacy Coaches ([LC_FTE] FTE each, [LC_QUALIFICATION]), who facilitate sessions and conduct home visits; a Family Outreach Coordinator ([FOC_FTE] FTE, [FOC_QUALIFICATION]), who manages recruitment, intake, and referral partnerships; and a Data and Evaluation Specialist ([DE_FTE] FTE, [DE_QUALIFICATION]), who oversees assessment administration and data analysis. All direct-service staff complete [TRAINING_HOURS] hours of training in [TRAINING_TOPICS] before delivering programming and receive [SUPERVISION_FREQ] reflective supervision throughout the grant.

The implementation timeline is as follows. Months 1–3 focus on hiring, training, partner onboarding, and first-cohort recruitment. Month 2 marks the launch of the first cohort's core programming. By month 6, all activity tracks will be fully operational and the second cohort will begin recruitment. A midpoint program review occurs in month 12, with data-informed adjustments implemented by month 14. Final cohorts complete programming by month 22, and months 22–24 are dedicated to exit assessments, follow-up planning, and final reporting. A detailed quarterly milestone table is included in Appendix [TIMELINE_APPENDIX].

# Section 6: Outcomes & Objectives (~400 words)

## Paste-Ready Version (No Subheadings)

Riverton Literacy Project has established four measurable objectives that correspond directly to the needs documented in Section 2 and the activities described in Section 4. Each objective follows a SMART framework — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound — and distinguishes between program outputs (services delivered) and participant outcomes (changes in knowledge, behavior, or status).

Objective 1 — Children's Foundational Literacy Skills. By month 24, at least [TARGET_RATE_1]% of participating children ages 0–8 will demonstrate measurable improvement in foundational literacy skills, moving from a baseline mean score of [BASELINE_SCORE_1] to a target mean score of [TARGET_SCORE_1] on the [MEASURE_TOOL_CHILD] assessment, administered at intake and again at the end of each 12-week cycle. Current community baseline data indicate that 28% of children in ZIP 12345 read below a sixth-grade functional literacy level; this objective targets a [POINT_REDUCTION]-percentage-point reduction among program participants.

Objective 2 — Caregiver Confidence and Home Literacy Practices. By month 24, at least [TARGET_RATE_2]% of participating caregivers will report increased confidence in supporting their child's literacy development, as measured by a pre/post score gain of [TARGET_GAIN_2] points or more on the [MEASURE_TOOL_CAREGIVER] scale. Additionally, [TARGET_RATE_2B]% of caregivers will report reading with their child at least [READING_FREQ] times per week at exit, up from a baseline of [BASELINE_RATE_2B]% at intake.

Objective 3 — Program Completion and Dosage. Over 24 months, Riverton Literacy Project will enroll 400 children and their caregivers across 10 cohorts. At least [RETENTION_RATE]% of enrolled families will complete the full 12-week cycle, defined as attending a minimum of [MIN_ATTENDANCE] of 12 sessions plus [MIN_HOMEVISITS] of 6 home visits. This output target ensures sufficient dosage to produce the literacy gains described in Objectives 1 and 2.

Objective 4 — Sustained Engagement After Exit. Within [FOLLOWUP_TIMELINE] after program completion, at least [TARGET_RATE_4]% of exited families will report continued use of at least one community literacy resource (e.g., library card activation, school reading program enrollment, ongoing story-time participation), as measured by a brief follow-up survey. This objective tests whether the program's transition planning in Phase 3 produces lasting behavioral change beyond the intervention period.

Together, these four objectives create a chain of accountability: Objective 3 confirms that services were delivered at sufficient intensity, Objectives 1 and 2 confirm that services produced measurable change, and Objective 4 confirms that change is durable. Baseline values for Objectives 1 and 2 will be established during the first cohort's intake assessments in months 1–3 and reported to the funder in the first quarterly report.

# Section 7: Evaluation Plan (~400 words)

## Paste-Ready Version (No Subheadings)

Riverton Literacy Project will conduct a mixed-methods evaluation using a pre-post design with repeated measures across all 10 cohorts. The evaluation serves two purposes: accountability (demonstrating whether outcomes were achieved) and learning (identifying what works, for whom, and why, so the program can improve in real time).

The evaluation design centers on three data collection points per family. At intake, staff administer the [MEASURE_TOOL_CHILD] to each child and the [MEASURE_TOOL_CAREGIVER] to each caregiver, establishing individualized baselines. At exit — the end of the 12-week cycle — the same instruments are re-administered to capture pre-post change. A third data point is collected [FOLLOWUP_TIMELINE] after exit via a brief follow-up survey assessing sustained literacy behaviors (Objective 4). This three-point structure allows Riverton Literacy Project to measure both immediate impact and short-term durability.

Data sources and instruments are as follows. Children's foundational literacy skills are measured by the [MEASURE_TOOL_CHILD], a [TOOL_VALIDATION_CHILD] instrument normed for [TOOL_NORMS_CHILD]. Caregiver confidence and home literacy practices are measured by the [MEASURE_TOOL_CAREGIVER], a [TOOL_VALIDATION_CAREGIVER] instrument, supplemented by [HOMEVISIT_NUM_SHORT] self-reported items on reading frequency. Program dosage and attendance are tracked through Riverton Literacy Project's [DATA_SYSTEM] database, updated by Literacy Coaches after each session and home visit. Qualitative data — caregiver testimonials, open-ended survey responses, and coach field notes — are collected continuously and coded thematically at midpoint and endline to surface contextual insights that quantitative data alone cannot capture.

The Data and Evaluation Specialist ([DE_FTE] FTE) is responsible for data management, quality assurance, and analysis. Quantitative analysis includes paired-sample comparisons of pre-post scores, calculation of effect sizes, and disaggregation by demographics, cohort, and dosage level to identify differential outcomes. Qualitative data are analyzed using thematic coding. [EXTERNAL_EVALUATOR] will provide [EXTERNAL_EVAL_ROLE] to ensure methodological rigor and independent validation of findings.

Results will be used in four ways. First, the Program Director reviews output dashboards monthly to monitor enrollment, attendance, and dosage. Second, the full team conducts a formal midpoint review at month 12, using cohort-level outcome data to adjust session content, outreach strategies, and coaching protocols before the next cohorts begin. Third, quarterly reports are submitted to the funder summarizing progress against all four objectives. Fourth, an end-of-grant summary report will be shared with [DISSEMINATION_AUDIENCES] to inform the broader field and support future funding applications. All participant data are stored in [DATA_SYSTEM], protected by [DATA_SECURITY_MEASURES], and de-identified before any external reporting, in compliance with [COMPLIANCE_STANDARD].
